items.title: Dick Griffin interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 12, 2024
items.q: And then the lady, her name was Miss Bessie Marino, and after a year of taking lessons with her she passed away.

ctx.x: What was the state of segregation in your neighborhood when you were the age that you’re talking about?

Oh ten or twelve — segregation was very prominent. When I say very prominent, we didn’t see like white people in our neighborhood hardly. None at night. Maybe during the day you might see one or two insurance salesmen or something, but the whole neighborhood was full of black people. And I could go weeks and days without seeing anybody black — I mean white. And, but going to school during the school time we had to pass through a white neighborhood and we never passed through that white © Fillius Jazz Archive -5-

neighborhood solo, alone. Because we would be maybe somebody’d come out and threaten us or run — you know little kids — run at us or something like that. But this guy named Herbert Delaney, he is deceased now, my best friend, my mentor, he was taking piano lessons. He had a piano and his family was — you know he had a mother and a father and his sister went to Alcorn College and everything, but I looked up to him. He was about four years older than me. My stepfather got killed when I was seven years old, and that…
